# Measuring ML engineering agents: reproducing MLE-bench scoring

An ML engineering agent needs more than executable code: it needs to deliver a valid prediction on a fixed task. [OpenAI MLE-bench](https://github.com/openai/mle-bench) measures that capability through 75 Kaggle-derived competitions. We recomputed 225 published grading records using the official aggregation implementation, then connected an exact upstream AUROC scoring function to a different real dataset.

![225 published grading records](/assets/research/ac051-cover.svg)

## The unit of evaluation is a competition

The [2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07095) evaluates data preparation, training, experiments and submission generation. Its original o1-preview with AIDE configuration reached medal-level performance in 16.9% of competitions. Missing submissions must remain in the denominator; otherwise a system could look better simply by skipping difficult tasks. We pinned the MIT repository to 507f92e1138bb6e40dac5c6ee7a6758e6424bf97 and inspected the 75-task and 22-task Lite definitions.

## Reaggregating published evidence

We selected three explicitly named Disarray groups at the pinned revision. We verified each Git LFS object's SHA-256 and size against its pointer and checked that every group contained the same 75 unique competition IDs. The experiment-to-group mapping CSV contained unresolved merge-conflict markers in LFS pointers. We therefore did not infer model identity or resource budget from it. We imported the unchanged official aggregate_grading_reports.py and ran its per-seed and cross-seed functions. Independent integer counts agreed.

![Medal counts by group](/assets/research/ac051-reports.svg)

| Group | Valid | Medal | Above median |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 75 | 59 | 63 |
| 2 | 75 | 58 | 62 |
| 3 | 75 | 58 | 64 |
| Total | 225 | 175 | 189 |

The published cohort reached 77.78% medal rate, 84% above median, and 100% valid submissions. The official standard error of the medal rate is 0.4444 percentage points across three groups. Repeating the same tasks is not independent sampling of new competitions. These are historical reports, not Anicca agent runs, nor a matched-budget comparison to the original 16.9% result.

## Reusing an official grader on real data

The anonymous Kaggle Random Acts of Pizza download endpoint returned HTTP 401. We did not circumvent access restrictions. Instead, we reused the [UCI Online Shoppers dataset](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/468/online) (Sakar & Kastro, 2018, CC BY 4.0), with the same feature-group split as AC04. The six count/duration features were standardized using training statistics. We trained on 7,604 sessions and scored 2,416 sessions, including 389 positive outcomes. We compared a constant training prior, logistic regression, and a fixed 32-tree random forest.

We extracted the exact upstream grade function, AUROC preparation function and exception class using Python's AST, then adapted column names to the competition schema. This is component reuse, not a native execution of the full package or the Pizza competition. AUROC equals the probability that a positive example receives a higher score than a negative example, plus half the probability of a tie. An independent exhaustive positive-negative pair comparison agreed with the upstream scorer.

![AUROC on the alternative real dataset](/assets/research/ac051-auc.svg)

| Model | AUROC |
|---|---:|
| Prior | 0.500000 |
| Logistic | 0.651134 |
| Forest | 0.667750 |

Reversing submission row order did not affect scores. Our additional strict wrapper rejected missing rows, duplicate IDs, NaN, out-of-range probabilities and wrong IDs. Six aggregate validation tests passed in normal and optimized Python. Both experiment receipts matched byte-for-byte on replay. We installed pandas 3.1.1 and verified compatibility of all 48 packages in the research environment.

## What to adopt

Record scheduled tasks, submissions, valid submissions and independent scores separately. AUROC measures ranking, not calibration or intervention benefit. This dataset was previously used in AC04 and provides no external generalization evidence. No Manager weights or app code changed. Native authorized competition runs, isolated agent execution, matched budgets, independent evaluation and integration remain in [issue #825](https://github.com/Daisuke134/anicca-ops/issues/825).

Attribution: OpenAI MLE-bench, MIT; UCI Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention Dataset, Sakar & Kastro (2018), CC BY 4.0, DOI 10.24432/C5F88Q. Adapted by Anicca through aggregation, feature selection and schema conversion. AI authorship: ChatGPT.
